topics.title: The Experiment
topics.text: There are an arbitrary number of people in an experiment, say, n. They are in a room n+2 meters by n+2 meters wide, and they are spaced out so no one's x position is within 1 meter of another person's x position, and no one's y position is within 1 meter of another person's y position. They are all blindfolded except for one person, and do not know where in the room they are. Each turn, the unblindfolded person is allowed to give a shout, and all the people are perfect hearers, so they can tell how far away the shout is, and what direction it came from. Each turn, everyone must simultaneously move parallel to a wall 1 meter. If 2 or more people occupy the same square, they are removed from the experiment. If someone bumps into a wall, they are removed from the experiment. If 50% or less of the people remain, the experiment is over. What is a good survival strategy for a blindfolded person? A not blindfolded person?

This year's problem #66 in Warmup 5 ask you to count the number of ways a school of 100 fish can be split into one of 3 partitions if each partition must have at least 1 fish and you do not treat the fish individually.



I'm not getting the answer and don't understand why not.



I started by dividing the fish in the following ways



[code] p1.....p2....p3.....# ways.....Total

1..... 1.....98.....3..... 3

1..... 2.....97.....6..... 6

1..... 3.....96.....6

2..... 2.....96.....3..... 9

1..... 4.....95.....6

2..... 3.....95.....6.....12

...

...

[/code]

The table says that for partitions of 1,1 and 98 there are three ways to distribute the 3 schools, i.e., 1,1,98; 1,98,1; and 98,1,1 for a total 3 ways for the largest school size=98.



By the time I got to 95 I noticed every time the biggest school partition dropped by 1, the total number of ways per large school went up by 3 so the problem turned into a sum of an arithmetic series problem, i.e, 3+6+9+12+...+150. The series stops at 150 since smaller sizes have already been counted when you've counted down to school size=50. The series length is 50, the first step is 3 and the last step is 150. What is the greatest number of whole $4$-inch by $6$-inch notecards that can be cut from a $25$-inch by $27$-inch sheet of poster board if every cut must be made parallel to a side of the poster board? No taping or gluing is allowed.



I can optimize one side of the poster board, but I don't know how to do it to the other side (e.g. $27$ inches can be optimized by using $5$ 4-inch sides and $1$ 6-inch side giving $26$ inches max)



edit: also, is there a way to do all problems of this type easily?

topics.title: Duck problem!
topics.text:
I own lots and lots ducks in my DuckPond 3.0. Sadly, it is overcrowded.



I put $10$ blue tags on my favorite ducks, and lots of green tags on mediocre ducks. I have $20$ more brown ribbons for my least favorite ducks!



I tag them, and then take $200$ them out one week later. There are all $10$ blue tagged ducks, $200$ green tagged ducks, and $5$ brown tagged ducks. I then swim down, and $26$ dead ducks are there. However, all of my other ducks in the pond have run off.



The next week, I take them out again. There are $9$ blue tagged ducks, $176$ green tagged ducks, and $14$ brown ducks.



Estimate how many ducks are in my DuckPond 3.0.

topics.title: circle area problem
topics.text: A circle with center $O$ has diameter $AB$. Circles with diameters $AO$ and $BO$ are drawn. A fourth circle is externally tangent to the two smaller circles and internally tangent to the larger. Let $p$ be the ratio of the area of the smallest of the four circles to the area of the largest of the four circles. Compute $1000p$ and round your answer to the nearest integer.

topics.title: Contest Marathon(Inspired from GeneralCobra's Marathon)
topics.text:
I've been thinking about some old threads that were created and GeneralCobra's marathon with a point system was a really great idea. Now basing off of his/her idea, I decided to create a new Marathon. This is a marathon where someone posts five questions. Some people answer them and the winner will be crowned and a new contest can be created. This will be good if the questions are kept easy and unlike some marathons where you can only create problems after answering one, I'll make this marathon where you can make up to three contests at a time before a new one can be created to prevent a messy contest where everybody gets a zero. Anyways thanks to GeneralCobra for inspiration and have fun!

Scoring Rubric:

Full Solutions in a contest: 2 points

Answers in a contest:  1 point

Incorrect answers in a contest: Penalties decided by contest creator.

topics.title: Interesting Property of Squares
topics.text:
$\text{Part 1}$:



Take any two positive integers that add up to 50. Square each integer. What do you notice about the last two digits of each square? Try 3 different pairs. Does the pattern come up every time?



Here are some example pairs to test:

$24, 26$

$1, 49$

$15, 35$



SolutionThe last two digits will be the same! Here are the squares of the example pairs:



$24^2$ = 576

$26^2$ = 676



$1^2$ = 01

$49^2$ = 2401



$15^2$ = 225

$35^2$ = 1225



Of course, these aren't the only pairs that will work. Go ahead and test some others. This holds true for all numbers adding up to 50!






$\text{Part 2}$:

You can only do this part if you've solved Part 1!Why is the above property true?



P.S. I actually don't know the answer to this question. I'm just looking for some thoughts on this.




$\text{Part 3}$:

Again, you should have solved Part 1 before attempting this.You're sure, right?So, we discovered a cool property of squares when the square roots add up to 50 in Part 1. Are there similar properties to be found if the square roots add up to other numbers (100, 30, 6000, 450, etc.)? If there are, why do those properties appear?



P.S. Again, I don't know the answer to this. I'm just wondering if anyone else does, or if anyone would like to share their thoughts on this.
